functional.text: Collect metrics (name, tags, timestamp, value) pushed by an agent on every host and service.
Query and graph metrics on dashboards: time range, aggregation (avg, sum, p99) and group by tag.
Alert rules (query + threshold + 'for' duration) notify on-call via PagerDuty, Slack or email; no duplicate pages.
Retention: raw 10 s data for 15 days, 1 min rollups for 30 days, 1 h rollups for 2 years.

non_functional.text: Ingest ~5M datapoints per second without losing data during spikes (write-heavy).
Dashboard queries p95 < 1 s for the last hour, a few seconds for long ranges.
Alerting fires within ~1 minute of a breach and stays available when the monitored systems fail.
Storage is cheap per point: compress and downsample instead of keeping raw forever.

assumptions.text: 100k hosts × ~500 series each, sampled every 10 s; 50M active series.
~5k open dashboards with ~20 panels refreshing every 30 s; ~50k alert rules.

out_of_scope.text: Logs, distributed traces and ML anomaly detection.

api.notes: Agents batch every 10 s; collectors ack after Kafka acks.
Resolution is chosen from the range and step.
Rules are assigned to an evaluator shard by id.

data.name: series_index
data.fields: series_id ↔ metric + sorted tags; inverted index tag=value → series ids
data.why: Turns {service=web} into the series ids to read.

data.name: datapoints
data.fields: series_id, timestamp, value in 2 h blocks (delta-of-delta ts, XOR values)
data.why: Append-only, compressed to ~1.5 B per point, sharded by series hash.

data.name: rollups
data.fields: series_id, bucket (1 min | 1 h), min, max, sum, count
data.why: Keep long ranges cheap; avg = sum / count stays correct when re-aggregated.

data.name: alert_rules / alert_state
data.fields: rule_id, query, condition, for, channels; state, since, fingerprint

deep_dives.title: High cardinality tags

options.name: Accept any tags
options.cons: a user_id or request_id tag creates millions of series and blows up the index and head block

options.name: Per-tenant series limits and a tag allowlist; reject or drop at the collector
options.cons: users must be told why data is missing

deep_dives.choice: Enforce per-tenant active-series limits at the collectors, drop unbounded tags (ids, URLs), and expose a cardinality report
deep_dives.why: Cost scales with the number of active series, not datapoints: one bad tag can add 10M series. Stopping it at ingest is the only place it is cheap.

deep_dives.title: Flapping and duplicate pages

options.name: Notify on every evaluation that breaches
options.cons: a value hovering at the threshold pages every 30 s; one outage fires 500 alerts

options.name: State machine with a 'for' duration, hysteresis, grouping and a dedupe key

deep_dives.choice: Pending → firing only after the 'for' duration; the notifier dedupes on (rule, labels) fingerprint and groups related alerts per service for 30 s
deep_dives.why: On-call trust is the product: fewer, correct pages beat fast noisy ones. The fingerprint also makes notifier retries idempotent.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Ingest writers and the TSDB head blocks (memory per active series), the series index under high cardinality, and the query fan-out across shards for wide queries.
wrapup.failures: Kafka buffers hours of data if the TSDB is down; writers replay from offsets. If a query shard is slow, return partial results with a warning. Alerting runs in its own cluster and a dead-man's-switch alert pages if the evaluators stop.
wrapup.monitoring: Monitor the monitor: ingest lag (Kafka consumer lag), dropped points, active series per tenant, query p95, evaluator loop duration vs interval, notification delivery failures. A second, small independent system watches this one.
wrapup.scale: 10×: more Kafka partitions and writers, more TSDB shards by series hash, rollups earlier; split tenants into separate cells.
wrapup.future: Logs and traces with shared tags, streaming evaluation for sub-10-second rules, anomaly detection, SLO burn-rate alerts.

parts.title: Ingestion pipeline
parts.problem: Accept ~5M datapoints per second from 100k host agents, survive spikes and storage hiccups without dropping data, and let more than one consumer read the same stream.

options.name: Agents write straight to the time-series store
options.cons: spikes and slow storage push back on every host; no replay; one consumer only

options.name: Pull: scrapers poll each target's /metrics endpoint
options.pros: the server controls the rate; a failed scrape is itself a signal; no buffering in agents
options.cons: needs service discovery and sharded scrapers; awkward across networks and for short-lived jobs

options.name: Push to stateless collectors that produce to a partitioned log
options.pros: absorbs spikes, replayable, many consumers (storage, streaming alerts, rollups)
options.cons: one more system to run; end-to-end lag of seconds

parts.choice: Agents push batches every 10 s to stateless collectors behind a load balancer; collectors validate and produce to Kafka partitioned by series hash; ingest writers consume per partition into the TSDB
parts.why: 5M points/s is ~80 MB/s of values (a few hundred MB/s on the wire with tag sets) and arrives in bursts (deploys, incidents). A log in the middle lets storage fall behind for minutes without losing data, and partitioning by series hash keeps each series on one writer so appends stay in order.

parts.title: Time-series storage and downsampling
parts.problem: Store 5M points/s cheaply: raw 10 s data for 15 days, 1 min rollups for 30 days and 1 h rollups for 2 years, with fast reads by series and time range.

options.name: Relational table (series_id, ts, value)
options.cons: ~16 B + index per row at 5M rows/s: index bloat and vacuum pain; no compression

options.name: Wide-column store (Cassandra) keyed by series and time bucket
options.cons: no native compression or downsampling; you build the TSDB on top

options.name: Purpose-built TSDB: in-memory head block, Gorilla-compressed immutable blocks, rollups to object storage
options.pros: ~1.5 B per point, append-only, fast range scans

parts.choice: TSDB sharded by series hash: in-memory head block, sealed 2 h blocks with delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-compressed values; a downsampler writes 1 min and 1 h rollups (min, max, sum, count) and moves old blocks to object storage
parts.why: Compression is the whole game: 5M × 86,400 × 15 days × 16 B ≈ 100 TB raw, but ≈ 10 TB compressed. Rollups make 30-day graphs read 1,440 points per series per day instead of 8,640, and object storage makes 2-year retention cheap.

parts.title: Query path for dashboards
parts.problem: Serve ~3k dashboard queries/s (auto-refreshing panels) in under a second, over ranges from 1 hour to 1 year, aggregating thousands of series by tag.

options.name: Always query raw data
options.cons: a 90-day panel over 1,000 series reads ~800M points

options.name: Pick resolution by range + scatter-gather over shards + result cache
options.pros: bounded points per query; refreshes hit the cache
options.cons: rollups lose detail (spikes inside a minute); cache invalidation for 'now'

parts.choice: Query service resolves tags to series ids through the series index, picks raw for ranges < 1 day and rollups otherwise, scatter-gathers across TSDB shards, and caches results by (query, step, aligned time window)
parts.why: A graph is ~1,000 pixels wide, so more than ~1,000 points per series is waste. Choosing the resolution by range keeps every query bounded, and most dashboard load is the same panels refreshing every 30 s, which a cache aligned to the step absorbs.

parts.title: Alert evaluation and notification
parts.problem: Evaluate ~50k alert rules every 30–60 s, fire within about a minute of a breach, avoid flapping and duplicate pages, and keep alerting while the systems being monitored are on fire.

options.name: Periodic evaluation: run each rule's query against recent data
options.pros: reuses the query language and path; simple state machine
options.cons: adds query load; detection latency = scrape + interval

options.name: Streaming evaluation on the ingest log (Flink)
options.pros: seconds of latency, no storage load
options.cons: windowed state per rule; complex rules (joins, ratios) are hard; harder to test

parts.choice: Periodic evaluation: evaluators shard the rules by id, query the hot tier every 30 s, keep per-rule state (ok → pending → firing → resolved) with a 'for' duration, and enqueue notifications; a notifier dedupes, groups and routes them
parts.why: 50k rules / 30 s ≈ 1.7k queries/s on recent, cached data is cheap, and one query language for dashboards and alerts avoids drift. The 'for' duration and grouping stop flapping and page storms; streaming stays an option for the few rules that need seconds.
